anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer, despite having usable statistics, chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan because of cost-model or plan-cache issues.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, creating system-wide compute contention that slows all workload components.

When these three root causes arise together, the database experiences extreme and erratic latency. Verbose or chatty SQL generated by the application multiplies the number of logical operations the optimizer must plan; a mischosen plan then inflates the physical work per statement—often turning what should be index seeks into full scans, spawning excessive parallel workers, or causing runaway nested-loop joins. The bloated execution demand drives CPU utilization to sustained saturation, pushing run-queue lengths and context switches high. Symptoms include: recurrent appearance of the same statements in slow-query and CPU-top lists, rapid oscillation between wildly different plans for identical SQL text, steep degradation after plan-cache invalidations or parameter shifts, widespread increases in service latency, and resource-wait events shifting from I/O to CPU-scheduler contention. Because CPU is the shared bottleneck, even well-written queries begin to stall, masking the original logical and planning flaws.

Causally, inefficient SQL logic supplies an overlarge search space to the optimizer; if the optimizer then selects or reuses a poor plan, per-statement CPU demand skyrockets. The inflated demand aggregates across many sessions, quickly exhausting CPU headroom. Once CPU is saturated, run-queue delays elongate execution times, which in turn keep transactions open longer, amplifying the footprint of the already chatty workload and further biasing the optimizer toward low-concurrency but high-CPU plans. This positive feedback loop intertwines the three anomalies, making remediation impossible unless all contributing layers—application SQL, plan stability, and CPU capacity—are addressed in concert.

entry.official_description: Cannot execute statement because it needs to be written to the binary log as multiple statements, and this is not allowed when @@SESSION.GTID_NEXT == 'UUID:NUMBER'.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with unsupported syntax, invalid statement structure, or feature usage that the target engine version cannot execute as written.
entry.solution_guidance: Validate SQL syntax, target-engine compatibility, statement shape, and whether the feature is supported under the current engine version or execution context.
